mechanism: Rifamycins are potent CYP3A4 (plus UGT and P-gp) inducers that accelerate metabolism of contraceptive oestrogen and progestogen, lowering plasma levels and risking contraceptive failure and unintended pregnancy.

management.prescriber_action: Recommend a contraceptive method unaffected by enzyme induction (copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUS, or DMPA injection) for the duration of rifamycin therapy and 4 weeks after; a short rifamycin course with a stable method may add non-hormonal precautions, but for long-term rifamycin additional short-term backup is NOT reliable, switch method.
management.patient_counselling: Hormonal contraception may fail during rifampicin/rifabutin and for about 4 weeks after stopping; use non-hormonal backup (condoms) or switch to an unaffected method; ask about emergency contraception if needed.
management.duration: Effect persists throughout rifamycin therapy and about 28 days after the last dose as enzyme activity recovers.
management.exceptions: Depot medroxyprogesterone (DMPA) injection and intrauterine methods (copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUS) are NOT clinically affected and are the preferred alternatives; do not extend this rule to non-hormonal methods.

mechanism: Enzyme-inducing antiepileptics induce CYP3A4 (and UGT), accelerating metabolism of contraceptive oestrogen and progestogen and reducing efficacy of combined and progestogen-only pills and progestogen implants.

management.prescriber_action: For ongoing enzyme-inducing antiepileptic therapy, recommend a contraceptive method unaffected by induction (copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUS, or DMPA injection) rather than relying on additional short-term precautions; oxcarbazepine, eslicarbazepine and topiramate above 200 mg/day are also relevant inducers to assess.
management.patient_counselling: These seizure medicines can make hormonal contraception fail; use an unaffected method or a reliable non-hormonal backup; discuss options with your prescriber.
management.duration: Effect persists while the inducing antiepileptic is taken and for about 4 weeks after stopping.
management.exceptions: Depot medroxyprogesterone (DMPA) injection and intrauterine methods (copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUS) are NOT clinically affected the same way and are preferred; non-enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (e.g. levetiracetam, lamotrigine, valproate) do not reduce contraceptive efficacy.

mechanism: Rifampicin potently induces CYP3A4 and P-gp, markedly reducing exposure of tacrolimus and ciclosporin and risking subtherapeutic immunosuppression and transplant rejection.

management.prescriber_action: Transplant/specialist team must anticipate large immunosuppressant dose increases with frequent therapeutic drug monitoring; avoid rifamycin where an alternative anti-infective exists. Do not withhold the immunosuppressant.
management.monitoring: Frequent tacrolimus/ciclosporin trough levels when rifampicin is started AND stopped; graft function.
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop your transplant medicine; attend for level checks; report rejection symptoms.
management.duration: Induction develops over 1-2 weeks and wanes over about 2 weeks after stopping rifampicin.
management.exceptions: Sirolimus and everolimus are affected similarly and also require monitoring.

evidence.normalized_proposition: Rifampicin lowers tacrolimus/ciclosporin exposure via CYP3A4/P-gp induction.

mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 and greatly reduces the oral bioavailability of verapamil (high first-pass metabolism), causing loss of rate and blood-pressure control.

management.prescriber_action: Oral verapamil may become ineffective; consider an alternative agent less dependent on CYP3A4 under specialist guidance.
management.monitoring: Heart rate, blood pressure, and anginal/arrhythmia control.
management.patient_counselling: Report palpitations, chest pain or uncontrolled blood pressure.
management.duration: Onset over 1-2 weeks; offset over about 2 weeks.
management.exceptions: Oral (high first-pass) verapamil is most affected; intravenous verapamil is less so.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - rifampin markedly reduces oral verapamil bioavailability>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Rifampicin markedly lowers oral verapamil exposure via CYP3A4 induction.

mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4, increasing clearance of systemic corticosteroids; this can cause loss of disease control and, where steroids are given as adrenal replacement, precipitate adrenal insufficiency or crisis.

management.prescriber_action: Corticosteroid dose commonly needs roughly doubling during rifamycin therapy; for adrenal replacement or transplant immunosuppression this is essential; specialist adjusts and reduces the dose when rifampicin stops.
management.monitoring: Disease control; signs of adrenal insufficiency in replacement-therapy patients.
management.patient_counselling: If your steroid is replacement therapy, do not stop it; seek urgent care for adrenal-crisis symptoms (severe weakness, vomiting, dizziness).
management.duration: Onset over 1-2 weeks; offset over about 2 weeks.
management.exceptions: Inhaled and topical corticosteroids are much less clinically affected.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - CYP3A4 inducers such as rifampin increase corticosteroid clearance>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Rifampicin lowers systemic corticosteroid exposure via CYP3A4 induction.

mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP2C9 (and CYP3A4), increasing sulfonylurea clearance and reducing glucose-lowering effect, risking loss of glycaemic control and hyperglycaemia (the opposite direction to CYP2C9-inhibitor hypoglycaemia).

management.prescriber_action: Anticipate loss of glycaemic control; monitor glucose and adjust antidiabetic therapy during and after the rifamycin course.
management.monitoring: Blood glucose and HbA1c during and after rifampicin.
management.patient_counselling: Check your blood sugars more closely; report persistent high readings.
management.duration: Onset over 1-2 weeks; offset over about 2 weeks.
management.exceptions: Gliclazide and glimepiride are CYP2C9-dependent; glibenclamide handling differs.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - CYP2C9 inducers such as rifampin may reduce sulfonylurea effect>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Rifampicin reduces sulfonylurea glucose-lowering effect via CYP2C9 induction.

mechanism: Rifampicin potently induces CYP3A4, UGT and P-gp, markedly reducing exposure of many antiretrovirals and risking virological failure and resistance; the magnitude and acceptability are agent-specific.

management.prescriber_action: HIV and TB specialists must select a compatible regimen, often substituting rifabutin for rifampicin and/or adjusting the antiretroviral; do not stop established antiretroviral therapy.
management.monitoring: HIV viral load per the HIV service.
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop your HIV medicines; adherence is critical; the specialist will reconcile the combination.
management.duration: Onset over 1-2 weeks; offset over about 2 weeks.
management.exceptions: Efavirenz and dolutegravir (with dose adjustment) may be co-administered; ritonavir/cobicistat-boosted regimens, rilpivirine, doravirine and bictegravir with rifampicin are contraindicated or not recommended - use rifabutin-based regimens under specialist guidance.

evidence.normalized_proposition: Rifampicin lowers antiretroviral exposure via strong induction; some boosted regimens are contraindicated.

evidence.normalized_proposition: Antiretroviral-rifamycin management is agent-specific; rifabutin often replaces rifampicin.

mechanism: Carbamazepine is a strong CYP3A4 (and P-gp) inducer that reduces exposure of tacrolimus and ciclosporin, risking subtherapeutic immunosuppression and transplant rejection.

management.prescriber_action: Anticipate higher immunosuppressant doses with frequent therapeutic drug monitoring; where feasible use a non-enzyme-inducing antiepileptic (e.g. levetiracetam). Do not withhold the immunosuppressant.
management.monitoring: Frequent tacrolimus/ciclosporin trough levels when carbamazepine is started AND stopped; graft function.
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop your transplant medicine; attend for level checks; report rejection symptoms.
management.duration: Onset over 1-3 weeks (with autoinduction); offset over 2-3 weeks.
management.exceptions: Sirolimus and everolimus are affected similarly and also require monitoring.

evidence.normalized_proposition: Carbamazepine lowers tacrolimus/ciclosporin exposure via CYP3A4/P-gp induction.

mechanism: Carbamazepine induces CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, increasing warfarin clearance and lowering INR with risk of subtherapeutic anticoagulation and thromboembolism.

management.prescriber_action: Anticipate a higher warfarin requirement with frequent INR, and a dose reduction when carbamazepine is stopped.
management.monitoring: INR after starting and after stopping carbamazepine, and frequently during titration.
management.patient_counselling: Keep INR appointments; report signs of clot (leg swelling, chest pain, breathlessness).
management.duration: Onset over 1-3 weeks; offset over 2-3 weeks.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - carbamazepine (CYP inducer) decreases warfarin effect and INR>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Carbamazepine lowers INR by inducing warfarin metabolism.

mechanism: Bidirectional: carbamazepine induction lowers verapamil exposure and rate/BP control, while verapamil (a CYP3A4 inhibitor) raises carbamazepine levels and can cause carbamazepine toxicity (diplopia, ataxia, sedation).

management.prescriber_action: If verapamil is added to carbamazepine, monitor for carbamazepine toxicity and check levels; if carbamazepine is added, monitor rate/BP control as verapamil may lose effect; consider alternatives to one agent.
management.monitoring: Carbamazepine level and toxicity signs; heart rate and blood pressure.
management.patient_counselling: Report double vision, unsteadiness or drowsiness (carbamazepine toxicity) and palpitations or uncontrolled blood pressure.
management.duration: Inhibition effect within days; induction over 1-3 weeks.
management.exceptions: The verapamil-raising-carbamazepine (inhibition) direction often dominates clinically.

evidence.normalized_proposition: Carbamazepine and verapamil interact bidirectionally (induction of verapamil; inhibition raising carbamazepine).

mechanism: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4, increasing clearance of systemic corticosteroids and risking loss of disease control or, for replacement therapy, adrenal insufficiency.

management.monitoring: Disease control; signs of adrenal insufficiency in replacement-therapy patients.
management.patient_counselling: If your steroid is replacement therapy, do not stop it; seek urgent care for adrenal-crisis symptoms.
management.duration: Onset over 1-3 weeks; offset over 2-3 weeks.
management.exceptions: Inhaled and topical corticosteroids are much less clinically affected.

mechanism: Carbamazepine induces sulfonylurea metabolism (CYP2C9/3A4), reducing glucose-lowering effect and risking loss of glycaemic control and hyperglycaemia.

management.prescriber_action: Anticipate reduced glycaemic control; monitor glucose and adjust antidiabetic therapy during and after carbamazepine changes.
management.patient_counselling: Check your blood sugars more closely; report persistent high readings.
management.duration: Onset over 1-3 weeks; offset over 2-3 weeks.
management.exceptions: Gliclazide and glimepiride are CYP2C9-dependent; glibenclamide handling differs.

mechanism: Complex bidirectional interaction: carbamazepine induces CYP3A4 and lowers exposure of many antiretrovirals (risking virological failure), while ritonavir/cobicistat inhibit CYP3A4 and raise carbamazepine levels (risking carbamazepine toxicity).

management.prescriber_action: HIV and neurology specialists must reconcile; prefer a non-enzyme-inducing antiepileptic (e.g. levetiracetam) or an antiretroviral regimen without this interaction; do not stop established antiretroviral therapy.
management.monitoring: Carbamazepine level and toxicity; HIV viral load.
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop your HIV medicines or your seizure medicine; the specialists will adjust the combination.
management.duration: Inhibition within days; induction over 1-3 weeks.
management.exceptions: Rilpivirine and doravirine with carbamazepine are contraindicated per label; ritonavir/cobicistat-boosted regimens and bictegravir are generally avoided; dolutegravir may be used only with a dose increase to twice-daily dosing.

evidence.normalized_proposition: Carbamazepine and boosted antiretrovirals interact bidirectionally; combination is generally avoided.

mechanism: Bidirectional: carbamazepine induces valproate metabolism (lowering valproate levels), while valproate inhibits epoxide hydrolase and raises the active carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide metabolite, causing toxicity even when the parent carbamazepine level is normal.

management.prescriber_action: Neurology to monitor both agents; be aware epoxide toxicity is not reflected in the parent carbamazepine level; adjust doses accordingly; do not stop either antiepileptic abruptly.
management.monitoring: Valproate and carbamazepine levels and clinical toxicity (the epoxide is not measured routinely).
management.patient_counselling: Report double vision, unsteadiness, drowsiness or breakthrough seizures; do not stop either seizure medicine.
management.duration: Effects develop over days to weeks.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - valproate raises carbamazepine-epoxide; carbamazepine lowers valproate>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Carbamazepine and valproate interact bidirectionally, including epoxide-mediated toxicity.

mechanism: Carbamazepine induces lamotrigine glucuronidation, lowering lamotrigine levels and efficacy; additive neurotoxicity (dizziness, diplopia) is also reported.

management.prescriber_action: Lamotrigine often needs a higher maintenance dose with carbamazepine; monitor seizure control and neurotoxicity and re-titrate if carbamazepine is stopped.
management.monitoring: Seizure control and neurotoxicity; lamotrigine level if available.
management.patient_counselling: Report increased seizures or dizziness/double vision; do not change doses on your own.
management.duration: Onset over 1-3 weeks; offset over 2-3 weeks.

evidence.excerpt: <verify - carbamazepine decreases lamotrigine concentrations (glucuronidation induction)>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Carbamazepine lowers lamotrigine exposure via UGT induction.

mechanism: St John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum, hyperforin) induces CYP3A4 and P-gp, reducing exposure of these substrates and causing therapeutic failure: transplant rejection (ciclosporin/tacrolimus), thromboembolism (DOAC/warfarin), unintended pregnancy (contraceptives) and virological failure (antiretrovirals).

management.prescriber_action: Advise against St John's Wort with these agents and refer; if already taken, anticipate loss of effect and monitor drug levels/effect; on stopping the herbal, induction wanes over 1-2 weeks and substrate levels may rise (e.g. ciclosporin toxicity).
management.monitoring: Substrate-specific: immunosuppressant levels, INR, HIV viral load.
management.patient_counselling: Do not take St John's Wort with these medicines; it can cause transplant rejection, clots, contraceptive failure or HIV treatment failure; tell your prescriber if you have been taking it.
management.duration: Induction onset and offset over about 1-2 weeks.
management.exceptions: Hyperforin content varies between products; low-hyperforin preparations induce less but cannot be assumed safe.
